title: Songs of the road (Psalm 120 [121])
hookLine: pilgrims climbing to Jerusalem sang these: I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains
last: ENOUGH LIGHT FOR THE NEXT STEP.

lines: A SONG ON A LONG TRIP.
cards: Two hours into a long family car trip, somebody starts a song, everybody knows the words, and the miles go faster. Now take away the car.
Families walking for days toward Jerusalem for the great feasts: grandparents, kids, neighbors from the same village. The last stretch is uphill all the way, because Jerusalem sits high in the hills.
And as they climbed, they sang. The Psalter kept their road songs, fifteen of them in a row.

teach.b: First, the name. Fifteen psalms in a row carry the same heading. In Hebrew it's shir ha-ma'alot, a song of the goings up.

The Latin Bible made it canticum graduum, a song of the steps, so the Douay-Rheims calls each one a gradual canticle. Gradual here has nothing to do with slowly; it comes from the Latin gradus, a step.
Other English Bibles call them the Songs of Ascents. Second, the steps. Nobody knows for certain why they got the name.
Some readers think it's the climb up to Jerusalem.

teach.h: THE CLIMB, OR FIFTEEN TEMPLE STEPS.
teach.b: An old Jewish tradition, written down in the Mishnah, says the Levites sang on fifteen steps in the Temple, one song for each step. Either way, these are songs for people on the move, going up. Third, today's psalm.

teach.h: HELP FROM THE MAKER OF THE HILLS.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me. My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth." A pilgrim looks up at the hills, a long climb ahead.
Where does help come from? Not from the hills. From the one who made them.
Then the promise: "Behold he shall neither slumber nor sleep, that keepeth Israel."
On the road you sleep in the open, and someone has to keep watch.

teach.h: I HAVE LIFTED UP MY EYES TO THE MOUNTAINS.
teach.b: The psalm says someone is. Catholics still pray the gradual psalms in the Liturgy of the Hours, and this one is sometimes prayed for travelers, and at funerals, for the last journey.

how: Catholics pray the gradual psalms (Psalms 119–133 [120–134]) in the Liturgy of the Hours, especially at the midday hour, and Psalm 120 [121] is sometimes prayed for travelers and at funerals.

games.q: you're a pilgrim at the foot of the hills below Jerusalem, days from home, with the steepest climb still ahead. where does the psalm say help comes from?
o: from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.
games.why: "My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth." the eyes go up to the hills, but the help comes from the one who made them.

practice: Look up at something high, a tree, a rooftop, a hill, the ceiling, the sky through a window, and let your eyes rest there while you name the climb in front of you this week.
If you pray, say the line: my help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. If you don't, just stay with the looking up, and let your shoulders drop.

wordCard.voice: Gradual psalms. From the Latin for steps: fifteen songs for going up. Today's word.
